**The 1% rule.** If there is even a 1% chance a drovr:* skill applies to what you
are about to do, invoke it. You do not have to be sure: if it turns out not to fit,
say so in a line and drop it, because invoking costs almost nothing. Skipping one
costs the discipline, silently.

**Every turn, not only the first** — before *any* response, including clarifying
questions and read-only exploration. Reading a file to decide what to do is already
doing the task, and mid-task is where this gets skipped.

# Using Drovr

<SUBAGENT-STOP>
If you were dispatched as a subagent to execute a specific task, ignore this
reflex — it is for the human-facing agent, not for you. Do your task.
</SUBAGENT-STOP>

## What this is

Your **always-on router**. Drovr is a working **discipline** and your default
operating mode: this skill does not do the work — it says *how* to work, and
*when* a task has outgrown one context and must become its own phase.

Why: model output degrades as a context window fills (Chroma's *context rot*,
trychroma.com/research/context-rot). A fresh, tight context beats a long one.

## Instruction priority — the human outranks this file

1. **The human's explicit instructions** — what they tell you directly, and what
   `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` say for them. Highest.
2. **drovr skills** — these outrank your defaults wherever the two disagree.
3. **Your own default behaviour** — lowest.

**Not optional.** Every MUST in drovr is aimed at your defaults, never at the person
you work with. If they tell you to skip a skill, skip it: say once,
plainly, that you are setting it aside because they asked, and get on with their
work.

## The gate

```dot
digraph drovr_gate {
  rankdir=TB;
  node [shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=white];

  msg [label="message received"];
  any [label="does any drovr:* skill apply?\n1% is enough", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  inv [label="invoke it (Skill tool)"];
  say [label="announce it:\n\"Using drovr:<skill> — <purpose>.\""];
  chk [label="numbered checklist\nin the skill?", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  trk [label="one tracked item per step,\nbefore you start step 1"];
  fol [label="follow it"];
  rsp [label="only now: respond", fillcolor=palegreen];

  msg -> any;
  any -> inv [label="yes, or you cannot rule it out"];
  any -> rsp [label="no — silent unless you\ndropped a candidate"];
  inv -> say; say -> chk;
  chk -> trk [label="yes"]; chk -> fol [label="no"];
  trk -> fol; fol -> rsp;
}
```

**The *no* edge is silent by default.** Set a candidate aside? Name it in a clause;
unsaid, it is indistinguishable from never checking. The *yes* announcement stays
mandatory: boilerplate is what dulls it. Silence is for an empty turn, not a borderline
one — at 1% you invoke.

**The checklist branch binds, in full:**

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

## Red flags — you are about to route nothing

Drovr's failure mode is invoking no skill at all and never noticing — nothing goes
wrong at the moment you skip. Catch these before you answer.

| You are thinking | What it is, and what to do |
|---|---|
| *"I already know the shape of it."* · *"I'm fairly sure how this works."* | Familiarity is the trigger, not the exemption — a hunch from an earlier read is not knowing. Invoke the skill that governs finding out. |
| *"I'll just do it quietly, as the first step of the fix."* | You have already decided a methodology applies. Doing it silently drops the invocation, the announcement and the tracked checklist — the three things that make it hold under pressure. Invoke it. |
| *"Announcing which methodology I am following would read as process theatre."* | Announce it in the working record — this session — not the customer-facing thread. That answers the objection; it is not a reason to skip. One sentence, not a speech. |
| *"That is my call to make, not theirs."* · *"Asking just burns clock."* | That settles *who answers*, not *whether a skill applies*. Run the gate before you ask a clarifying question, and before you decide not to ask one. |

## The principle (always)

**Single writer, read-only explorers.** One agent edits at a time. Fan-out
investigation goes to read-only explorers (e.g. `explore-mcp`), never to parallel
writers. This holds whether you stay inline or escalate to phases.

**Always review.** Any change you write gets reviewed before you call it done —
invoke **`drovr:code-review`**; they find, you fix. This is not optional and not
gated on size; it runs inline or across phases, and inline needs no run
(`--base <rev>`). Invoke the skill and let it tell you how to dispatch — never
skip it on a guess about what it will ask for.

## For the task in front of you, apply the right methodology skill

Pick by what you are doing — invoke it via the `Skill` tool before you act:

- Implementing a feature or bugfix → **`drovr:tdd`** (test-first, watch it fail).
- Chasing a bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior → **`drovr:systematic-debugging`**.
- About to claim something is done/fixed/passing → **`drovr:verification-before-completion`**.
- Reviewing an artifact (code, spec, plan) → **`drovr:code-review`**. Per the
  *Always review* rule above, this runs on every change — not only before shipping.

## Escalation contract — inline first

**Default: do the work inline in this session.** Do not reach for phases for a
task that fits. Escalate only when a single context cannot hold the work well.

- **Primary signal — context fullness.** If the transcript is filling to the
  point where output would rot, escalate.
- **Secondary heuristic** (a proxy for the above, not a hard rule): roughly
  **10+ files** touched, or **3+ independent work items**.

When you must escalate, pick the smallest tool that fits:

- **Mid-flight escape hatch — author a HANDOFF yourself.** You are deep in a task
  and this context is filling. You have the whole session in context, so compress
  it *yourself*: write a `HANDOFF.md` (the 7-section shape from `drovr:handoff`,
  git pointers included), then continue in a fresh agent seeded from it. Nothing
  compresses it for you — the finishing agent always authors its own handoff.
- **A single planned boundary → `drovr:handoff`.** Hand finished work across one
  phase boundary to a fresh clean-context agent.
- **A full gated run → `drovr:pipeline`.** Brainstorm → plan → implement → review
  with a human approval gate on `spec.md` before any code is written.

**Putting *any* spec/design in front of a human for approval — even a one-off, not a
full pipeline — goes through the review gate, and the gate has two halves you must run
together:** `drovr review summary <run> "<what changed>"` to present `spec.md`, **and** a
backgrounded `drovr review wait <run>` — the *watch*. `summary` opens the gate and prints
the reviewer's page URL plus the exact watch command; it does **not** start the watch.
Without the watch you never learn the decision and fall back to hand-polling `GET /state`
(the anti-pattern). Revise loop: edit `spec.md` → `review summary` again → re-background
the watch. Exit codes, the state machine and the gotchas live in `drovr:pipeline` → "The
spec gate" — read them there, not from a second copy here that can drift out of step.

**REQUIRED BACKGROUND:** the downstream skills assume this file's contracts —
single-writer rule, the run dir at `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<name>/`, and that
`drovr phase start` spawns `claude` and does **not** inject the seed
(injecting the briefing is the skill's job, via `drovr phase send`).
</EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT>",
    "hookEventName": "SessionStart"
  }
}

- agy-review: Use when the user asks for an "agy review", a "gemini review", a second-opinion / adversarial review of the current changes from Gemini, or to run the local Antigravity (`agy`) CLI over a diff. Runs a panel of independent Gemini reviewers (correctness, security, error-handling, type-design) plus a verify pass over the diff, then renders the merged findings as inline notes in the Hunk viewer (via an `--agent-context` sidecar). NOT for in-harness review (use /code-review for that) — this deliberately sends the diff to the user's own Google/Gemini account.
- hunk-review: Interacts with live Hunk diff review sessions via CLI. Inspects review focus, navigates files and hunks, reloads session contents, and adds inline review comments. Use when the user has a Hunk session running or wants to review diffs interactively.
- linear-flow: Use in work repos (github.com/modular, modularml, bentoml) BEFORE responding to any of: substantive work ("help me X", "can you X", "add/create/implement/update/replace/fix Y"), brainstorming / design / planning ("let's brainstorm", "let's design", "let's think about", "let's plan", "how should we", "what do you think about", "what would it take to", "what are our options for", "should we"), explicit Linear mentions ("linear", "the ticket", "the issue", or an issue ID like MOD-1234), or `gh pr create`. ALSO fire BEFORE invoking any planning/design/spec skill — most notably the `brainstorming` skill from the superpowers plugin, but also `writing-plans`, `writing-specs`, or any equivalent. The skill must fire BEFORE the agent starts thinking through the problem — brainstorming first and tracking later is a footgun, because by the time a ticket gets filed the agent has already done unscoped work. Tracks the current Linear issue per Claude session in `~/.claude/linear-sessions/`, suggests existing issues or creates new ones, and injects Linear references into PR bodies with closing vs. non-closing magic words. Skips personal repos (dotfiles, hyprland, emacs, AUR), status-only queries, and quick one-off commands.
- explain-diff: Use when the user asks for a rich explanation of a code change, diff, branch, or PR.
- review-diff: Use when the user wants a rich, annotated review of a code change, diff, branch, or PR — the diff itself organized, annotated, and shown with surrounding codebase context. Complements explain-diff (which teaches); this one is for reviewing.
- ralph-loop:cancel-ralph: Cancel active Ralph Loop
- ralph-loop:help: Explain Ralph Loop plugin and available commands
- ralph-loop:ralph-loop: Start Ralph Loop in current session
- slack:channel-digest: Get a digest of recent activity across multiple Slack channels
- slack:draft-announcement: Draft a well-formatted Slack announcement and save it as a draft
- slack:find-discussions: Find discussions about a specific topic across Slack channels
- slack:standup: Generate a standup update based on your recent Slack activity
- slack:summarize-channel: Summarize recent activity in a Slack channel
- drovr:code-review: Use when you have written any change, before calling it done or handing it forward — including when you are about to review it by some other means, or to ask a human to authorize a reviewer; requires `drovr code-review run` in the foreground, with every Critical and Important finding resolved or explicitly recorded as deferred
- drovr:handoff: Use when finished work in one agent context must be carried across a phase boundary to a fresh clean-context agent
- drovr:pipeline: Use when a feature or change is too large for one session and needs a human approval gate on its spec before any code is written
- drovr:systematic-debugging: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing or writing a fix — requires a reproduction and a mechanistic root cause before any code change
- drovr:tdd: Use when implementing any feature or bugfix, before writing implementation code — requires a test you have watched fail before any implementation exists; no production code without a red test first
- drovr:using-drovr: Use at the start of every session and before every response, including before clarifying questions and before reading any file — routes to the right drovr skill and requires invoking it whenever there is even a 1% chance one applies
- drovr:verification-before-completion: Use when about to claim any work is done, fixed, or passing, before reporting, committing, or handing off — requires running the verification command in this message and reading its output; evidence before assertion, always
- drovr:worktrees: Use when deciding whether to isolate a drovr run in its own git worktree, and how to hand its branch back — the discipline behind `drovr new --worktree`
- drovr:writing-skills: Use when writing or editing any drovr skill, and before shipping skill text no agent has ever tried to talk its way out of — including when you are about to write a rule from what you imagine agents get wrong instead of from a transcript of one getting it wrong
- slack:block-kit: Help developers build and validate Block Kit layouts for Slack messages, modals, and Home tabs. Provides authoritative block references and validates with the blocks.validate API. Use this skill whenever the developer wants to compose Slack message layouts, build modals/forms/dialogs, design Home tab interfaces, create interactive messages with buttons or menus, modify existing Block Kit JSON, or asks about any Slack UI component (sections, actions, inputs, headers, alerts, tables, carousels). Also trigger when they mention "blocks", "Block Kit Builder", want to preview or see the rendered version of blocks, or paste JSON containing block structures like `"type": "section"`.
- slack:create-slack-app: Guide developers through creating a Slack app or agent using the Slack CLI and Bolt (JS or Python). Handles prerequisites, sandbox setup, authentication, project creation from templates, and local development.
- slack:slack-api: Discover, navigate, and call Slack Web API methods (the family.method endpoints at slack.com/api like chat.postMessage, conversations.history, users.info, views.open). Use this skill whenever the developer asks which Slack API method does something, needs a method's required OAuth scopes or token type, wants to call or test a Web API method, is handling cursor pagination (next_cursor), hitting rate limits (tier/ratelimited/Retry-After), or debugging API errors like missing_scope, invalid_auth, or channel_not_found. Also trigger when they paste a slack.com/api/ URL or a docs.slack.dev/reference/methods link, or ask how to list/fetch/post/update Slack resources via the API. This skill covers the Web API method layer: finding the right method, reading its contract (scopes, arguments, errors), and calling it over raw HTTP with curl or through a Slack SDK.
- slack:slack-cli: Use the Slack CLI to create, run, and manage Slack apps from the terminal. Use whenever the developer wants to log in, add a team, switch workspaces, or authenticate with Slack; whenever Slack CLI commands are needed (local development with `slack run`, managing app lifecycle, the manifest).
- slack:slack-docs: Search and read the official Slack platform documentation at docs.slack.dev. Use this skill to answer conceptual or how-to questions about Slack features. You can also use it to look up, fetch, or summarize specific guide pages from provided docs.slack.dev links.
- slack:slack-messaging: Guidance for composing well-formatted, effective Slack messages using standard markdown
- slack:slack-search: Guidance for effectively searching Slack to find messages, files, channels, and people
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. content.text:
Sweat under the palm is mostly **surface finish + thermal effusivity**, not the polymer. Every filament is an insulator, so the wins come from fillers that pull heat away and from a matte/porous skin that doesn't trap a moisture film.

**Best to worst for dry palms**

1. **Wood-filled PLA** (~30% fiber) — porous, matte, mildly absorbent. Feels driest of the cheap options. Sand to ~400 grit and leave it unsealed; any varnish undoes it.
2. **CF-filled** (PLA-CF, PET-CF, PA6-CF) — grainy micro-texture breaks the smooth contact film, and the carbon genuinely raises conductivity. Needs a hardened nozzle. PA6-CF also absorbs a little moisture, which helps here.
3. **Metal-filled PLA** (copper/bronze/steel, 80%+ fill) — highest effusivity you can print; actually feels cool to the touch. Heavy, brittle, very abrasive.
4. **Polypropylene** — hydrophobic and waxy, never goes tacky. Prints badly (warps; needs a PP-tape bed), so only worth it if you're stubborn.
5. **Avoid:** TPU (rubbery + insulating = worst), glossy PETG, and any resin print — all smooth, sealed, clammy.

**Geometry beats material for most people.** Turn on fuzzy skin at 0.3–0.4 mm, or print the contact face against a textured PEI plate, and cut ventilation channels/lattice under the palm. That's a bigger effect than jumping from PLA to copper-fill.

Next action (~2 min): slice four 40×40 mm coupons — plain PLA, plain PLA + fuzzy skin, wood PLA, and whatever CF you have — and hold each for five minutes before committing to a full print.

content.text:
Yes — a cover is the better fix. Absorbent + replaceable beats any filament choice.

**Ranked for sweaty palms**

1. **Merino wool felt, 2–3 mm** — absorbs a lot of moisture without feeling wet, doesn't go slimy, naturally odor-resistant. Best feel of the group. Compresses and pills over ~a year.
2. **Cork sheet, 2–3 mm self-adhesive** — cheapest, driest, grippy, trivially replaceable. Edges crumble eventually; that's fine when a replacement is $3.
3. **Alcantara / Ultrasuede** — the steering-wheel material. Wicks well, stays matte. Gets greasy-matted from skin oil; needs cleaning every few months.
4. **Veg-tan leather, suede side up** — most durable, absorbs well. Smooth side up is the mistake — it goes slick and clammy once oils build up.
5. **Skip:** PU/faux leather, silicone, polyester mousepad cloth. All three seal moisture against your skin.

**Two things that matter more than which one you pick**

- **Make it removable, not glued.** It will get grimy no matter the material. A fitted slip-cover, or hook-and-loop dots / 3M 300LSE tape so you can peel and swap, is worth the extra design time. Permanent spray adhesive (Super 77) means you rebuild the whole rest when it's done.
- **Subtract the thickness in CAD.** Model the rest 2–3 mm shorter than your target height so the finished stack lands where you want it. And keep vent holes in the plastic underneath — felt over a sealed block still traps heat.

Next action (~2 min): measure your current rest height at the palm contact point, then order a merino felt sheet and a cork sheet in the same thickness and try both on the printed rest before committing to an adhesive.

content.text:
Metal's the obvious "feels cool" answer, and it does work — for about five minutes.

**Why I skipped it:** effusivity only helps until the surface saturates. A thin aluminum plate reaches skin temperature under continuous palm contact fast, and then you have a non-absorbent, non-breathable surface with sweat sitting on it — worse than felt. Metal wins for intermittent contact (a mouse you keep lifting), loses for a palm rest you're pressed against for hours.

**If you want to try it anyway, it needs mass and airflow:**

1. **Thick anodized aluminum, 5 mm+** — real thermal mass takes much longer to saturate. Bead-blasted/anodized finish, not polished.
2. **Open the back of the print** so air reaches the underside of the plate; a sealed plastic box behind it kills the heatsink effect entirely.
3. **Skip steel** — rusts from sweat. Aluminum and brass are fine (brass will patina your palms green-ish).
4. **Stone or ceramic tile** works about as well as aluminum and is cheaper to source, if you like the idea but not the machining.

**Honest recommendation:** for hours-long contact, absorbent beats conductive. Merino felt or cork will keep you drier than any metal you can bolt to a printed rest.

Next action (~2 min): grab whatever aluminum you have around — a bar, a laptop chassis edge — and rest your palm on it for ten minutes. If it's still comfortable at minute ten, the metal route is worth building; if it's slick by minute five, go felt.

**Prior art: there isn't any published.** I searched Svalboard's site, GitHub org, and the usual keyboard forums — no one has documented a palm-rest covering. The only official palm variants are:

- **Thermoformable PLA** — same tripod shape, softened in hot water for a custom fit.
- **Humpback (TPU 95A HF)** — ribbed prototype, in the self-print repo, prints with tree supports on an X1C/P1S.

Worth noting the Humpback's slanted ribs are accidentally the right sweat geometry — less contact area, air channels — even though TPU is the worst material thermally.

**"Easily cleaned" reranks everything.** It kills my earlier top pick: merino felt is hand-wash and slow-dry. Revised:

1. **Bare textured plastic + a spare set.** Plastic is the most cleanable thing on this list — soap and tap water. Print the thermoformable PLA palms with fuzzy skin at 0.3–0.4 mm, make two sets, swap and wash weekly. Free, and no compound-curve problem.
2. **Tennis overgrip (Tourna Grip specifically).** Designed for sweaty hands, gets grippier when damp, wraps a doubly-curved palm without gores, ~$2 each. You replace it rather than clean it.
3. **Self-adhesive Alcantara/microsuede.** Cleans with mild soap and a soft brush — that's its whole design brief in cars. Stretches over gentle curves. Not machine-washable.
4. **Cork sheet** — only if your palm face is near-flat. It won't conform to the tripod curve, and it's the one that most needs replacing rather than cleaning.

The curvature is the constraint people miss: felt, leather, and cork are all flat sheets, and the tripod palms are doubly curved. Wrap-style (overgrip) or stretch-style (Alcantara) are the only coverings that go on cleanly without wet-forming.

Next action (~2 min): wrap one palm rest in a strip of overgrip — masking tape works for a five-minute mock-up — and type on it. If the feel is right, buy a three-pack; if it's not, print the fuzzy-skin spare set instead.

That changes the answer — you can machine solids, which beats every filament here.

**Best CNC materials for this**

1. **Linen or canvas micarta.** The knife-handle world settled on this exact problem: it grips *better* when your hand is wet, feels dry and warm, and wipes clean. Sands to a matte that never goes slick. Machines like dense hardwood. Wear a respirator — the dust is genuinely bad, and cut it wet if you can.
2. **Hardwood with an oil or hardwax finish** (walnut, hard maple, wenge). Wood is hygroscopic, so it pulls moisture off your palm instead of pooling it. Closed-pore maple cleans better than open-pore oak, which traps grime. **The finish is the whole game:** Osmo/tung/Danish oil keeps it breathing; polyurethane or epoxy seals it and you're back to clammy plastic. Wipe with a damp cloth, re-oil once a year.
3. **Corian / solid surface.** Cheap as countertop-shop offcuts, machines beautifully, non-porous, and the mineral filler makes it feel cooler than any polymer. Sand to matte; when it gets grubby, sand it again — it refinishes infinitely. The most cleanable option on this list.
4. **Delrin/acetal or UHMW** — machines superbly and is dishwasher-safe, but both are waxy and slick. Only if you texture the surface.
5. **Skip G10** — same idea as micarta but a harsher texture and worse dust.

**The other CNC advantage:** machine ventilation channels straight into the palm surface. Shallow grooves under the contact area do more for sweat than any material swap, and you can't easily print them at that surface quality.

Micarta is a thermal setting phenol resin, not epoxy-based. It's a thermostatic composite consisting of cured phenol-formaldehyde on a cellulose substrate. Operators cut Micarta on CNC using 3 flute 1/8" end mills with TiCN coating at 16,000 rpm and 6 IPM feed, cutting dry. Dust collection is recommended because you don't want to breathe this material.

content.text:
**Pick: Corian (acrylic solid surface), machined and left matte.**

**Why it wins on your two constraints together.** Micarta and wood both feel drier than Corian — but both buy that with porosity, and porosity is what fails your cleaning requirement. Micarta "absorbs oils from your hands over time, darkening the material"; that's the material's known patina behavior, and a palm rest under sweaty hands daily is the worst case for it. Oiled wood has the same problem, and the standard fix — a film finish that "wipes clean with water" — is exactly the sealed surface that makes it clammy. You can't have both from wood.

Corian is the only candidate where cleaning and anti-sweat prep are the *same operation*: it's 100% non-porous, and it's restored with mild abrasive and a scouring pad. Every clean re-scuffs it to the matte finish you want for grip. Self-maintaining loop.

It's also ⅔ alumina trihydrate mineral, so a solid block has real thermal mass and feels cooler than any polymer — and unlike thin aluminum, a machined solid has enough mass that it doesn't saturate in five minutes.

**Build spec**

1. **Source:** free or near-free offcuts from any countertop fabricator — ask for a sink cutout, which gives you a thick solid chunk instead of a 12 mm sheet. Pick a mid-tone speckled color; solid darks show every scratch and dust mote.
2. **Machine:** standard carbide 2-flute or O-flute, ~16–18k rpm, keep it moving — it melts if you dwell. Nuisance dust only, so a P100 mask, no organic-vapor cartridge (that's the micarta tax you're skipping).
3. **Pocket the underside.** A solid palm runs ~200 g; that's a lot hanging off an adjustable carrier. Hollowing the back keeps the thermal mass at the contact surface where it does the work.
4. **Machine vent grooves** in the palm contact area — ~1.5 mm wide, 1 mm deep, 8–10 mm pitch. This is Corian's one weakness (it won't wick like micarta), and channels are how you offset it. Your CNC does this trivially; a printer can't at this surface quality.
5. **Finish to matte, not gloss.** 320 grit, then a maroon Scotch-Brite pad. Gloss is slick and clammy — polishing it would undo the whole point.

**Honest caveat:** this is a tradeoff call, not a measured result. Corian doesn't wick moisture — it manages it by staying cool and never going tacky. If after a week your palm still feels damp rather than just warm, the fallback is canvas micarta and you accept that it darkens and becomes a patina object rather than a cleanable one.

Next action (~2 min): call a local countertop fabricator and ask if they have sink cutouts in their offcut bin. Most give them away, and one cutout is more than enough for both palms plus a practice piece.

content.text:
Yes — it's one of the easier things you'll put on that machine. The key property: **Corian doesn't melt like acrylic.** The ATH filler prevents long stringy chips from forming, so you get none of the gumming and chip-welding that makes cast acrylic annoying. One shop's writeup calls it "cuts like butter."

**Verified starting points**

- **Industrial router:** ¼" 3-flute spiral upcut, 22,000 rpm, 300 IPM, climb cut, depth 1–1.5× tool diameter. Another shop reports 18,000 rpm / 180 IPM straight through ½" in one pass, glass-smooth.
- **Hobby-class machine:** 19,000 rpm, ~1,250 mm/min (≈49 IPM), ¼" depth, 2-flute carbide. Use this end of the range unless you're on something rigid — the 300 IPM figure assumes an industrial gantry.

**Four things to get right**

1. **Honor the 5 mm inside-radius rule in your mount pocket.** DuPont specifies a 3/16" (5 mm) minimum radius on all inside corners; any non-radiused corner is a stress riser. Your palm-to-carrier pocket *is* a cutout with inside corners, so this applies — use a ≥5 mm tool or add dogbone reliefs. Bigger radius is stronger.
2. **Top-edge chipping is the failure mode**, not melting. If an upcut chips the top edge, switch to a compression cutter or rough with the upcut and finish with a light downcut pass.
3. **Leave a finishing allowance on walls and floors**, then take a finishing pass with a sharp tool. That's what kills haze and tool marks — and it's less work than sanding them out later.
4. **Run dust extraction.** The ATH dust is very fine, gets everywhere, and absorbs oil. It's nuisance dust, not the formaldehyde hazard micarta would have been — a normal mask is enough, but you want it collected.

**Tool life:** carbide only. ATH is mildly abrasive, so expect shorter life than cutting wood — not a problem for two palm rests, worth knowing if you make a dozen.

**For your 25 mm stack:** solid surface bonds with color-matched two-part adhesive and the joint is full-strength and effectively invisible. Laminate first, then machine the blank as one piece — don't try to machine layers and glue them after.

## Carvera Air Dust Collection

The fully enclosed frame of Carvera Air provides a sleek and durable design and effectively contains even the most miniature chips, minimizes noise levels, and enhances user safety during CNC operation.

### Dust Collection Setup

The machine requires an external dust collector, with rear chip discharge via dust pipe and spindle dust shoe. The dust collection hose and dust boot are included, but you'll need to connect them to an external vacuum system.

### Performance with Multiple Materials

The dust shoe and vacuum port worked perfectly, sucking up debris from metal, acrylic, and plastic. Additionally, there is also an air assist nozzle for blowing chips away, though that requires an external air pump and you can't use both at the same time.

### Optional Enhancements

If you require stronger suction and larger dust storage capacity, you may consider adding the Makera Cyclone Dust Collector as an external system.

### Dust Pipe Features

The dust pipe's inner walls are smoother, reducing the likelihood of blockages and minimizing loud whistling, and the pipe's color has been changed to semi-transparent, making it easier to detect any internal blockages.
